docs.title: MCP TUI Test
docs.text:
Like Playwright, but for Terminal User Interfaces

An MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that enables AI assistants to test Terminal User Interface (TUI) applications. This server provides tools to launch, interact with, and verify TUI applications programmatically.

Get started See examples Codemode guide

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Dual Testing Modes: Choose between stream mode (for CLI tools) or buffer mode (for full TUIs with position awareness)
  • Launch TUI Applications: Start any terminal-based application with configurable dimensions
  • Send Keyboard Input: Simulate user typing, special keys, and control combinations
  • Capture Screen Output: Read and analyze the current terminal display
  • Position-Based Testing: Verify text at specific screen coordinates (buffer mode)
  • Cursor Tracking: Monitor cursor position in real-time (buffer mode)
  • Wait for Text: Asynchronously wait for specific content to appear
  • Assertions: Verify that expected content is present in the output
  • Session Management: Run multiple TUI applications simultaneously

docs.title: Stream Mode (Default)
docs.text:
• Best for: CLI tools, command-line applications, simple interactive programs
  • Uses: pexpect for stream-based testing
  • Features: Text matching, pattern waiting, output capture
  • Example use cases: git, npm, grep, interactive shell scripts

docs.title: Buffer Mode
docs.text:
• Best for: Full TUI applications, ncurses apps, dialog boxes, menus
  • Uses: pexpect + pyte for screen buffer emulation
  • Features: All stream features PLUS position-based assertions, cursor tracking, region extraction
  • Example use cases: htop, vim, dialog, interactive menus

When to use which mode: - Use stream mode for applications that output text sequentially - Use buffer mode for applications that draw complex UIs with cursor movement

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or higher
  • uv

docs.title: Install Dependencies
docs.text:
uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -r requirements.txt

Or install the package:

uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -e .

docs.title: Running the MCP Server
docs.text:
python server.py

Or if installed as a package:

mcp-tui-test

docs.title: Configure in Claude Desktop
docs.text:
Add this to your claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "tui-test": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["/path/to/mcp-tui-test/server.py"]
    }
  }
}

Or if installed as a package:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "tui-test": {
      "command": "mcp-tui-test"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: launch_tui
docs.text:
Launch a TUI application for testing.

Parameters: - command (required): The command to launch the TUI application - session_id (optional): Unique identifier for this session (default: "default") - timeout (optional): Command timeout in seconds (default: 30) - dimensions (optional): Terminal dimensions as WIDTHxHEIGHT (default: "80x24") - mode (optional): Testing mode - "stream" or "buffer" (default: "stream")

Examples: 

# Stream mode for CLI tools
launch_tui(command="python example_tui_app.py", session_id="test1")

# Buffer mode for full TUI applications
launch_tui(command="htop", session_id="test2", mode="buffer", dimensions="120x40")

docs.title: send_keys
docs.text:
Send keyboard input to a TUI application.

Parameters: - keys (required): Keys to send. Use \n for Enter, \t for Tab, \x1b for Escape - session_id (optional): Session identifier (default: "default") - delay (optional): Delay in seconds after sending keys (default: 0.1)

Example: 

send_keys(keys="1\n", session_id="test1")

docs.title: send_ctrl
docs.text:
Send a Ctrl+Key combination to the TUI application.

Parameters: - key (required): The key to combine with Ctrl (e.g., 'c', 'd', 'z') - session_id (optional): Session identifier (default: "default")

Example: 

send_ctrl(key="c", session_id="test1")

docs.title: capture_screen
docs.text:
Capture the current screen output of a TUI application.

Parameters: - session_id (optional): Session identifier (default: "default") - include_ansi (optional): Whether to include ANSI escape codes in stream mode (default: False) - use_buffer (optional): Force buffer/stream mode. Auto-detects if None (default: None)

Examples: 

# Auto-detect mode based on session
capture_screen(session_id="test1")

# Force buffer mode capture
capture_screen(session_id="test1", use_buffer=True)

docs.title: expect_text
docs.text:
Wait for specific text to appear in the TUI output.

Parameters: - pattern (required): Text or regex pattern to wait for - session_id (optional): Session identifier (default: "default") - timeout (optional): Maximum time to wait in seconds (default: 10)

Example: 

expect_text(pattern="Welcome", session_id="test1", timeout=5)

docs.title: assert_contains
docs.text:
Assert that the current screen contains specific text.

Parameters: - text (required): Text to search for in the current screen - session_id (optional): Session identifier (default: "default") - use_buffer (optional): Check buffer/stream mode. Auto-detects if None (default: None)

Example: 

assert_contains(text="Counter value: 1", session_id="test1")

docs.title: assert_at_position (Buffer Mode Only)
docs.text:
Assert that specific text appears at a screen position.

Parameters: - text (required): Text to verify at the position - row (required): Row number (0-indexed) - col (required): Column number (0-indexed) - session_id (optional): Session identifier (default: "default")

Example: 

# Verify "Error" appears at row 5, column 10
assert_at_position(text="Error", row=5, col=10, session_id="test1")

docs.title: get_cursor_position (Buffer Mode Only)
docs.text:
Get the current cursor position.

Parameters: - session_id (optional): Session identifier (default: "default")

Example: 

get_cursor_position(session_id="test1")
# Returns: "Cursor position (session: test1): row 10, column 25"

docs.title: get_screen_region (Buffer Mode Only)
docs.text:
Extract a rectangular region of the screen.

Parameters: - row_start (required): Starting row (0-indexed, inclusive) - row_end (required): Ending row (0-indexed, exclusive) - col_start (optional): Starting column (0-indexed, inclusive, default: 0) - col_end (optional): Ending column (0-indexed, exclusive, default: end of line) - session_id (optional): Session identifier (default: "default")

Example: 

# Extract rows 5-10, full width
get_screen_region(row_start=5, row_end=10, session_id="test1")

# Extract rows 5-10, columns 20-60
get_screen_region(row_start=5, row_end=10, col_start=20, col_end=60, session_id="test1")

docs.title: get_line (Buffer Mode Only)
docs.text:
Get a specific line from the screen buffer.

Parameters: - row (required): Row number (0-indexed) - session_id (optional): Session identifier (default: "default")

Example: 

get_line(row=3, session_id="test1")
# Returns: "Line 3 (session: test1): [line content]"

docs.title: close_session
docs.text:
Close a TUI testing session.

Parameters: - session_id (optional): Session identifier (default: "default")

Example: 

close_session(session_id="test1")

docs.title: list_sessions
docs.text:
List all active TUI testing sessions.

Example: 

list_sessions()

docs.title: Example Test Scenario
docs.text:
Here's how you might use this MCP to test a TUI application:

  1. Launch the application: 

    launch_tui(command="python example_tui_app.py")

  2. Wait for it to load: 

    expect_text(pattern="Welcome to the Example TUI Application")

  3. Interact with it: 

    send_keys(keys="1\n")

  4. Verify output: 

    assert_contains(text="Hello, TUI Tester!")

  5. Clean up: 

    close_session()

docs.title: Testing the Example App
docs.text:
This repository includes an example TUI application (example_tui_app.py) that you can use to test the MCP server.

Run it directly: 

python example_tui_app.py

Or test it through the MCP: 

launch_tui(command="python example_tui_app.py")
send_keys(keys="1\n")
capture_screen()

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Automated Testing: Verify TUI applications behave correctly
  • Integration Testing: Test command-line tools and interactive CLIs
  • Documentation: Generate screenshots and examples from TUI apps
  • Debugging: Inspect the state of TUI applications during development
  • CI/CD: Add TUI testing to your continuous integration pipeline

docs.title: Technical Details
docs.text: This MCP server uses: - FastMCP: For the MCP server implementation - pexpect: For spawning and controlling terminal applications - pyte: For terminal emulation and screen buffer management (buffer mode) - ScreenSession wrapper: Combines pexpect and pyte for hybrid testing

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Stream Mode: pexpect directly captures output stream
  • Buffer Mode: pexpect output → pyte terminal emulator → screen buffer
  • Auto-detection: Tools automatically use appropriate mode based on session

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Currently designed for Unix-like systems (Linux, macOS)
  • Windows support may require modifications (consider using winpty or similar)
  • Mouse support in TUIs is not currently available
  • Buffer mode requires slightly more memory for screen emulation
  • Position-based assertions only work in buffer mode

docs.title: Author
docs.text: Created for testing TUI applications with AI assistance.

docs.title: Composing TUI tests in a coding harness
docs.text:
Armin Ronacher's “What is Codemode” (2026-10-06) describes running orchestration code in the agent harness and calling tools from that code. Applied to this project, it favors small TUI tools with predictable structured results. The harness owns loops, branching, filtering, and orchestration; this server owns the terminal processes and their screen state.

The existing tools already expose MCP outputSchema and structuredContent. There is no need for an additional server-side JavaScript execution tool. A harness can call these tools alongside its other tools without nesting one interpreter inside another.

docs.title: Result contract
docs.text:
Use result.structuredContent for programmatic decisions. The serialized JSON text in content is provided for compatibility. The MCP tools specification defines this distinction.

Python and Go return the same set of fields for each tool on success and failure:

  • error is a string when an operation fails and null otherwise.
  • Assertion found and screen_excerpt are always present. null means no value; an empty string is an actual observation and must not be omitted.
  • list_sessions.sessions is always an array, including when empty, and reaped is always an object mapping removed session IDs to reasons.
  • success: false reports an operation failure. An assertion can return success: true, passed: false: the check ran, but the expectation did not hold.
  • expect_text.outcome distinguishes found, timeout, eof, and error.

Also handle a rejected tool call or MCP isError response: argument validation and transport failures can happen before a typed application result exists.

docs.title: A composed interaction
docs.text:
This example uses the article's JavaScript harness conventions (tools and text). Tool prefixes depend on how your harness names the connection; discover its tools and substitute the actual names. This code runs in that harness, not in Node.js or in the TUI server.

function checked(result) {
  if (result.isError) throw new Error(JSON.stringify(result.content));
  const data = result.structuredContent;
  if (!data || !data.success) {
    throw new Error(data?.error || data?.outcome || "Tool call failed");
  }
  return data;
}

// Choose a fresh ID: launching an existing ID replaces that session.
const session_id = "codemode-example-1";
checked(await tools.mcp__tui_test__launch_tui({
  command: "/bin/sh -c 'printf READY; read answer; printf DONE; read finish'",
  session_id,
  mode: "stream",
}));
try {
  checked(await tools.mcp__tui_test__expect_text({
    session_id, pattern: "READY", timeout: 5,
  }));
  checked(await tools.mcp__tui_test__send_keys({
    session_id, keys: "hello\n", raw: true,
  }));
  checked(await tools.mcp__tui_test__expect_text({
    session_id, pattern: "DONE", timeout: 5,
  }));
  const assertion = checked(await tools.mcp__tui_test__assert_contains({
    session_id, text: "DONE",
  }));
  // Return just the decision; keep full screens out of the model context unless needed.
  text({ passed: assertion.passed, excerpt: assertion.screen_excerpt });
} finally {
  const closed = await tools.mcp__tui_test__close_session({ session_id });
  if (closed.isError || !closed.structuredContent?.success) {
    text({ cleanupError: closed.structuredContent?.error || closed.content });
  }
}

docs.title: Ordering and execution boundaries
docs.text:
Await dependent operations on a session in order. Keyboard input, reads, waits, and lifecycle operations all touch mutable state; concurrent calls on the same session have no guaranteed ordering. Different session IDs can represent independent workflows, but concurrency support and throughput differ between implementations. The Python server's synchronous handlers can block other requests while waiting. Do not rely on another parallel call to unblock a waiting expect_text.

Bound loops and timeouts, stay within the configured session cap (eight by default), and close each session in finally. Reusing an ID is not an idempotent retry: a launch replaces its process and repeated key presses repeat their effects. Session IDs can be saved by a harness, but sessions are in memory, have a TTL, and do not survive a server restart.

Commands execute on the MCP server's host, with that host's filesystem and permissions. A sandbox around the harness's JavaScript does not sandbox the TUI process. Text screen captures and tui://{session_id}/screen resources cross the MCP boundary; local paths alone do not transfer files to a separate harness host.

docs.title: Contract verification
docs.text:
tests/test_protocol.py launches real servers over stdio, discovers the output schemas, and validates structured results and compatibility text. CI runs the same checks against both Python and the compiled Go binary. Locally:

uv venv && uv pip install -e ".[dev]"
(cd go && go build -o /tmp/mcp-tui-test ./cmd/mcp-tui-test)
MCP_TUI_TEST_BINARY=/tmp/mcp-tui-test uv run pytest tests/test_protocol.py -v

docs.title: TUI Testing Examples
docs.text: This document provides practical examples of using the MCP TUI Test server in both stream and buffer modes.

docs.title: Stream Mode Examples
docs.text: Stream mode is ideal for CLI tools and applications that output text sequentially.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic CLI Testing (Stream Mode)
docs.text:
Testing the included example TUI application:

# Launch in stream mode (default)
launch_tui(command="python example_tui_app.py")

# Wait for the welcome message
expect_text(pattern="Welcome to the Example TUI Application")

# Select option 1 (Say Hello)
send_keys(keys="1\n")

# Verify the greeting appears
assert_contains(text="Hello, TUI Tester!")

# Select option 3 (Counter)
send_keys(keys="3\n")

# Verify counter incremented
assert_contains(text="Counter value: 1")

# Quit the application
send_keys(keys="q\n")

# Close the session
close_session()

docs.title: Example 2: Testing Git Commands (Stream Mode)
docs.text:
# Launch git in stream mode
launch_tui(command="git status", session_id="git_test")

# Wait for output
expect_text(pattern="On branch", session_id="git_test", timeout=5)

# Capture the output
capture_screen(session_id="git_test")

# Close session
close_session(session_id="git_test")

docs.title: Example 3: Interactive Shell Script (Stream Mode)
docs.text:
# Launch an interactive script
launch_tui(command="./interactive_setup.sh", session_id="setup")

# Answer prompts
send_keys(keys="yes\n", session_id="setup")
expect_text(pattern="Enter your name:", session_id="setup")

send_keys(keys="Alice\n", session_id="setup")
expect_text(pattern="Enter your email:", session_id="setup")

send_keys(keys="alice@example.com\n", session_id="setup")

# Verify completion
assert_contains(text="Setup complete", session_id="setup")

close_session(session_id="setup")

docs.title: Buffer Mode Examples
docs.text: Buffer mode is ideal for full TUI applications with cursor positioning and screen layouts.

docs.title: Example 4: Testing TUI Menus (Buffer Mode)
docs.text:
# Launch in buffer mode for position-aware testing
launch_tui(command="python menu_app.py", mode="buffer", session_id="menu")

# Wait for menu to render
expect_text(pattern="Main Menu", session_id="menu")

# Verify title is at the top
assert_at_position(text="Main Menu", row=0, col=0, session_id="menu")

# Navigate menu with arrow keys
send_keys(keys="\x1b[B", session_id="menu")  # Down arrow
send_keys(keys="\x1b[B", session_id="menu")  # Down arrow

# Check cursor moved
cursor_pos = get_cursor_position(session_id="menu")
# Should show cursor at row 2

# Select menu item
send_keys(keys="\n", session_id="menu")

close_session(session_id="menu")

docs.title: Example 5: Testing Dialog Boxes (Buffer Mode)
docs.text:
# Launch dialog application in buffer mode
launch_tui(
    command='dialog --msgbox "Hello World" 10 30',
    mode="buffer",
    session_id="dialog",
    dimensions="80x24"
)

# Wait for dialog to appear
expect_text(pattern="Hello World", session_id="dialog")

# Verify message is centered (approximately row 5)
region = get_screen_region(row_start=3, row_end=7, session_id="dialog")
# Region should contain "Hello World"

# Press Enter to close
send_keys(keys="\n", session_id="dialog")

close_session(session_id="dialog")

docs.title: Example 6: Testing htop (Buffer Mode)
docs.text:
# Launch htop in buffer mode
launch_tui(
    command="htop",
    mode="buffer",
    session_id="htop",
    dimensions="120x40"
)

# Wait for it to render
expect_text(pattern="CPU", session_id="htop", timeout=5)

# Verify CPU header is at top
assert_at_position(text="CPU", row=0, col=0, session_id="htop")

# Get the header region
header = get_screen_region(row_start=0, row_end=5, session_id="htop")

# Should contain CPU, Mem, Swp

# Navigate with keys
send_keys(keys="t", session_id="htop")  # Toggle tree view
send_keys(keys="u", session_id="htop")  # Filter by user

# Quit htop
send_keys(keys="q", session_id="htop")

close_session(session_id="htop")

docs.title: Example 7: Position-Based Assertions (Buffer Mode)
docs.text:
# Launch application with structured layout
launch_tui(
    command="python dashboard.py",
    mode="buffer",
    session_id="dash",
    dimensions="100x30"
)

# Wait for dashboard to load
expect_text(pattern="Dashboard", session_id="dash")

# Verify title at specific position
assert_at_position(text="Dashboard", row=0, col=35, session_id="dash")

# Check status indicator at bottom right
assert_at_position(text="Status: OK", row=29, col=80, session_id="dash")

# Extract sidebar (first 20 columns)
sidebar = get_screen_region(
    row_start=1,
    row_end=28,
    col_start=0,
    col_end=20,
    session_id="dash"
)

# Sidebar should contain menu items
assert "Menu" in sidebar
assert "Settings" in sidebar

# Get specific line
line_5 = get_line(row=5, session_id="dash")

close_session(session_id="dash")

docs.title: Example 8: Cursor Tracking (Buffer Mode)
docs.text:
# Launch text editor
launch_tui(
    command="nano test.txt",
    mode="buffer",
    session_id="nano",
    dimensions="80x24"
)

# Wait for nano to start
expect_text(pattern="GNU nano", session_id="nano")

# Type some text
send_keys(keys="Hello, World!", session_id="nano")

# Check cursor position (should have moved)
pos = get_cursor_position(session_id="nano")
# Should show cursor moved to the right

# Move cursor with arrows
send_keys(keys="\x1b[D" * 6, session_id="nano")  # Left arrow 6 times

# Check cursor moved back
pos = get_cursor_position(session_id="nano")

# Exit without saving
send_ctrl(key="x", session_id="nano")
send_keys(keys="n\n", session_id="nano")

close_session(session_id="nano")

docs.title: Example 9: Testing Multiple Sessions
docs.text:
Running multiple TUI apps simultaneously:

# Launch first app in stream mode
launch_tui(command="python cli_tool.py", session_id="app1")

# Launch second app in buffer mode
launch_tui(
    command="htop",
    session_id="app2",
    mode="buffer",
    dimensions="120x40"
)

# List active sessions
list_sessions()
# Should show: app1 (stream), app2 (buffer)

# Interact with first app
send_keys(keys="status\n", session_id="app1")
assert_contains(text="Running", session_id="app1")

# Interact with second app
send_keys(keys="t", session_id="app2")
assert_at_position(text="CPU", row=0, col=0, session_id="app2")

# Close both sessions
close_session(session_id="app1")
close_session(session_id="app2")

docs.title: Example 10: Region Extraction for Comparison (Buffer Mode)
docs.text:
# Launch application
launch_tui(
    command="python status_app.py",
    mode="buffer",
    session_id="status"
)

# Wait for initial render
expect_text(pattern="System Status", session_id="status")

# Capture initial state of status region
initial_status = get_screen_region(
    row_start=10,
    row_end=15,
    col_start=0,
    col_end=50,
    session_id="status"
)

# Trigger a change
send_keys(keys="r", session_id="status")  # Refresh

# Wait a moment
send_keys(keys="", session_id="status", delay=1.0)

# Capture updated state
updated_status = get_screen_region(
    row_start=10,
    row_end=15,
    col_start=0,
    col_end=50,
    session_id="status"
)

# Compare regions
if initial_status != updated_status:
    print("Status region changed as expected")

close_session(session_id="status")

docs.title: Example 11: Testing Progress Bars (Buffer Mode)
docs.text:
# Launch app with progress bar
launch_tui(
    command="python download_simulator.py",
    mode="buffer",
    session_id="progress"
)

# Wait for progress bar to appear
expect_text(pattern="Downloading", session_id="progress")

# Check progress bar at specific line
progress_line = get_line(row=5, session_id="progress")

# Should contain progress indicator like [====    ] 50%
assert "[" in progress_line

# Wait for completion
expect_text(pattern="Complete", session_id="progress", timeout=30)

# Verify final progress
final_progress = get_line(row=5, session_id="progress")
assert "100%" in final_progress

close_session(session_id="progress")

docs.title: Example 12: Using Control Keys (Both Modes)
docs.text:
# Stream mode example - canceling a process
launch_tui(command="python long_running_task.py", session_id="task")

# Let it run for a bit
send_keys(keys="", session_id="task", delay=2.0)

# Cancel with Ctrl+C
send_ctrl(key="c", session_id="task")

# Verify cancellation
assert_contains(text="Cancelled", session_id="task")

close_session(session_id="task")

# Buffer mode example - quitting htop
launch_tui(command="htop", mode="buffer", session_id="htop2")

expect_text(pattern="CPU", session_id="htop2")

# Quit with 'q' key
send_keys(keys="q", session_id="htop2")

close_session(session_id="htop2")

docs.title: When to Use Stream vs Buffer Mode
docs.text:
Use Stream Mode for: - Command-line tools (git, npm, curl) - Simple interactive scripts - Applications that primarily output text - When you only need to check if text appears (not where)

Use Buffer Mode for: - Full-screen TUI applications (htop, vim, nano) - Applications with menus and dialogs - When you need to verify layout and positioning - When you need cursor position tracking - Applications that use ncurses or similar

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Add appropriate delays: Some TUI apps need time to render 

    send_keys(keys="command\n", delay=0.5)

  2. Use expect_text for async operations: When waiting for slow operations 

    expect_text(pattern="Done", timeout=30)

  3. Capture screen on failure: For debugging 

    try:
    assert_at_position(text="Expected", row=5, col=10)
except:
    debug_output = capture_screen(use_buffer=True)
    print(debug_output)

  4. Test with appropriate terminal sizes: Match your target environment 

    launch_tui(command="app", dimensions="132x43")  # Larger terminal

  5. Use sessions for isolation: Each test can have its own session 

    launch_tui(command="test1", session_id="test1")
launch_tui(command="test2", session_id="test2")

  6. Clean up sessions: Always close when done 

    try:
    # ... test code ...
finally:
    close_session(session_id="test")

docs.title: Wait and Verify Pattern
docs.text:
launch_tui(command="app", mode="buffer")
expect_text(pattern="Ready")
send_keys(keys="action\n")
assert_at_position(text="Success", row=10, col=0)
close_session()

docs.title: Region Comparison Pattern
docs.text:
launch_tui(command="app", mode="buffer")
before = get_screen_region(row_start=5, row_end=10)
send_keys(keys="update\n")
after = get_screen_region(row_start=5, row_end=10)
assert before != after
close_session()

docs.title: Multi-Step Workflow Pattern
docs.text:
launch_tui(command="wizard", mode="buffer")

# Step 1
expect_text(pattern="Step 1")
send_keys(keys="value1\n")

# Step 2
expect_text(pattern="Step 2")
send_keys(keys="value2\n")

# Step 3
expect_text(pattern="Step 3")
send_keys(keys="value3\n")

# Verify completion
assert_contains(text="Complete")
close_session()

docs.title: TUI-testing landscape
docs.text: Other tools that drive or snapshot terminal programs, what each one is built on, and the ideas in each that are worth isolating. Repository facts (stars, last push, language, dependencies) were read from the repositories themselves on 2026-10-26. Where a line says mcp-tui-test: it describes what this project does today; see the synthesis for the aggregate view.

docs.title: How mcp-tui-test fits
docs.text: mcp-tui-test spawns the program under test in a real PTY (pexpect in Python, creack/pty in Go) and optionally feeds its output through a VT emulator (pyte in Python, vt10x in Go) to get a screen grid. It exposes that as MCP tools with structured results, as a tui://{session_id}/screen resource, and as a pytest fixture. It has text and regex waits, substring and position assertions, region and line reads, cursor position, and session caps and reaping. It has no idle or stable-screen wait, no style or colour reads, no mouse or resize, no screenshots or recordings, no snapshot comparison, and no scrollback.

docs.title: microsoft/tui-test
docs.text:
github.com/microsoft/tui-test (formerly microsoft/shell-use; the old URL redirects) · Rust · 295 stars · pushed 2026-10-23.

  • Approach: real PTY on Windows, Linux and macOS, with a selectable emulator backend: Alacritty (default), Ghostty, Rio or xterm.js. One engine behind a CLI and in-process Rust, Python, JavaScript and Go libraries.
  • Assertions and snapshots: Playwright-style text locators (find/expect/click/highlight text) with regex, whitespace, style (--fg, --bold, …), OSC 8 link and before/after-anchor filters; expect snapshot NAME; waits on idle, title, clipboard, bell, command, exit and shell readiness; cells X Y W H returns styled cells.
  • Capture: SVG and PNG screenshots; APNG, GIF, MP4 and asciinema recordings; on-failure traces (trace.md, trace.json, timeline.json, trace.html).
  • Agent integration: agent-context prints the command schema as JSON, skill --add installs an agent skill, --json everywhere, and a session daemon so each CLI call is one step.

Core ideas:

  1. Locators over the screen grid instead of byte-stream matching. A locator is a query (text, regex, style, link, anchor) that resolves to cell spans and is retried until it passes. mcp-tui-test: has assert_contains and assert_at_position, but no query that returns match coordinates and no style or anchor filters.
  2. One engine, many front ends. The CLI and four language bindings share one native core, so a test written for an agent and a test in a cargo test behave identically. mcp-tui-test: has the same shape in miniature (MCP server and pytest fixture share core.py), but Python and Go are separate implementations that share only the tool schema.
  3. Failure artefacts for agents first. A failed assertion writes structured artefacts, and the docs tell agents to read trace.md and the JSON rather than the HTML. mcp-tui-test: attaches screen_excerpt to a failed assertion and nothing else.
  4. Swappable real emulators. Backends are real terminal cores, so a test can be run against the emulator a user actually has. mcp-tui-test: one fixed emulator per language.

docs.title: antithesishq/bombadil
docs.text:
github.com/antithesishq/bombadil · Rust · 1,564 stars · pushed 2026-10-23 · manual.

  • Approach: property-based testing of web and terminal UIs. Terminal mode runs the program on a real PTY (portable-pty) and parses its output with libghostty-vt. The loop is: extract state, check every property, pick the next action from the current state, perform it, wait for the next chunk of output or a timeout, repeat.
  • Assertions: properties are TypeScript modules using temporal operators (always, eventually, next, now, implies) over a sequence of states. Terminal defaults include exitSuccess and noReplacementChars; the default action generator types Unicode input and escape sequences. bombadil terminal shrink reduces a violating trace to a shorter one (marked experimental).
  • Results: Oskar Wickström's 2026-04-30 write-up reports a freeze in vitetris, two btop bugs (one already fixed in 1.4.6, one newly reported) and an rlwrap segfault from a few days of random input, scrolling and resizing at roughly 300 captured states per second.
  • Agent integration: none; it is a CI and local tool with a GitHub Action.

Core ideas:

  1. Property-based exploration instead of scripted examples. Random, state-aware action generation reaches sequences nobody scripted. mcp-tui-test: every action is chosen by the caller.
  2. Temporal properties over a state sequence. Invariants are checked after every step, not at one chosen moment. mcp-tui-test: single-moment assertions only.
  3. Shrinking a violating trace. A long random trace is reduced to a minimal reproduction. mcp-tui-test: no trace recording, so nothing to shrink.
  4. Default properties that need no spec. "Exits zero" and "never prints a byte the terminal can't render" catch real bugs with zero configuration. mcp-tui-test: no built-in invariants.

docs.title: montanaflynn/headless-terminal (ht)
docs.text:
github.com/montanaflynn/headless-terminal · Go · 121 stars · pushed 2026-08-31.

  • Approach: a Unix-socket daemon owns one PTY per session and feeds output through libghostty-vt (statically linked via cgo); the ht CLI talks JSON lines to it. Vim-style key notation (<CR>, <Esc>, <C-c>).
  • Assertions and snapshots: ht view in plain, ANSI, HTML, PNG or JSON; ht wait on text, cursor, idle, change or exit; asciicast recording via ht record; ht watch streams a session live to another pane.
  • Agent integration: an Anthropic-format skill in skills/headless-terminal/ that teaches the key notation and a "wait-strategy decision tree (the part agents get wrong)".

Core ideas:

  1. Send synchronisation as a first-class concept. Default 20 ms keystroke pacing, plus --wait-text, --wait-cursor, --wait-idle, --wait-change and --wait-exit that compose with AND on the same send. mcp-tui-test: send_keys sleeps a fixed delay (default 0.1 s); waiting is a separate expect_text call and only on text.
  2. Daemon-owned sessions, thin CLI. Sessions outlive any one command, so an agent issues one shell command per step. mcp-tui-test: equivalent via the MCP server process holding sessions.
  3. Shoulder-surfing. ht watch lets a human see live what the agent is driving. mcp-tui-test: no live view.
  4. Skill as the integration surface. Instead of an MCP server, a SKILL.md that teaches an agent when and how to call the CLI. mcp-tui-test: MCP tools only; no skill file.

docs.title: beorn/termless
docs.text:
github.com/beorn/termless · TypeScript (Bun and Node) · 36 stars · pushed 2026-10-24.

  • Approach: a TerminalBackend interface with twelve implementations: xterm.js (default), Ghostty via WASM, Ghostty native, Alacritty, WezTerm, vt100 (TypeScript), vt100 (Rust), vt220, vterm.js, libvterm, Kitty and Peekaboo (drives a real macOS terminal through accessibility APIs). Tests can feed() bytes with no process, or spawn() a real PTY (Bun native, or node-pty on Node).
  • Assertions and snapshots: region selectors (screen, scrollback, buffer, viewport, row(n), cell(r, c), range) and 21+ Vitest matchers for text, cell style, cursor, mode, title, scrollback and toMatchTerminalSnapshot(); term.out matches raw protocol bytes that render nothing (Kitty graphics, OSC 52). SVG and PNG screenshots; recordings in a .tty/.ttyz journal format with codecs to asciicast, .tape and ttyrec.
  • Agent integration: @termless/cli ships termless record, termless play and an MCP server.

Core ideas:

  1. Multi-backend conformance. The same test runs against every emulator, and a differential corpus mined from the emulators' own test suites grades backends against each other. mcp-tui-test: pyte and vt10x are implementation details, not selectable, and never compared.
  2. Three inlets, one path. feed(), spawn() and a replayed recording all arrive at the backend as ordered byte writes, so an assertion written against a live process runs unchanged against a stored journal. mcp-tui-test: live PTY only.
  3. Region selectors separate "where" from "what". expect(term.row(0)) and expect(term.cell(0, 8)).toHaveFg(…) compose a location with a matcher. mcp-tui-test: get_screen_region and get_line return text; there is no cell-level style view.
  4. Raw-output assertions for invisible protocol. Some behaviour changes no cell, so the byte stream stays inspectable next to the grid. mcp-tui-test: stream mode exposes the stream with ANSI optionally retained, but not alongside a grid in the same session.

docs.title: vyncint/termlens
docs.text:
github.com/vyncint/termlens · Rust · 27 stars · pushed 2026-10-23 · recommended in ratatui's snapshot-testing recipe as the PTY layer to pair with TestBackend.

  • Approach: real PTY, vt100 crate behind an internal trait (with a second parser recovering blink, conceal and strikethrough, which vt100 drops). A reader thread drains the PTY continuously and answers the queries a real terminal would answer (cursor position, DA, DECRQM, XTGETTCAP, background colour), so capability-probing apps do not hang. Every Screen is an immutable snapshot taken under one lock. Windows via ConPTY.
  • Assertions and snapshots: wait_until(pred), wait_frame(pred) for complete DEC 2026 synchronized frames, snapshot_after(pred), wait_stable, wait_idle, wait_exit; assert_screen_snapshot! via insta; mask_matching, mask_rect and mask_matches blank volatile cells on the grid without shifting columns; Screen::diff reports cell-by-cell changes; Screen::parse reads a printed snapshot back in. Mode-aware input: mouse, paste and keys are encoded for the modes the app enabled. graphics() captures Kitty and sixel transmissions. A termlens CLI does inspect, diff and render --svg.
  • Agent integration: none beyond the CLI and JSON output (serde feature).

Core ideas:

  1. Wait on a predicate over the screen, not on text. Every wait takes a closure over the full Screen (cells, styles, cursor, modes, counters) and is deadline-bounded with the screen attached on timeout; there is no sleep. mcp-tui-test: expect_text waits on a regex over the stream; the pytest plugin's wait_until_contains polls the buffer text.
  2. Frame-complete snapshots. wait_frame returns only complete DEC 2026 frames, so a snapshot is never torn mid-repaint; snapshot_after waits for the predicate and then for stillness. mcp-tui-test: capture_screen reads whatever has arrived.
  3. Mask the grid, not the text. Volatile content is replaced cell-for-cell so layout and styles still compare. mcp-tui-test: no snapshot comparison.
  4. Answer the terminal's questions. Replying to capability probes is what lets real apps run under a fake terminal. mcp-tui-test: pexpect and pyte do not answer CSI 6n or DA requests; apps that wait for a reply stall until their own timeout.

docs.title: mwunsch/termscope
docs.text:
github.com/mwunsch/termscope · Zig · 19 stars · pushed 2026-04-08.

  • Approach: single static binary on libghostty-vt. termscope snapshot -- cmd for one-shot capture, termscope exec with --wait-for-text, --type, --press, --wait-idle, --expect for scripted runs, and termscope session as a JSON-lines request/response protocol over stdin/stdout. Emacs-style key notation (C-c, M-x, RET).
  • Assertions and snapshots: --expect TEXT sets the exit code; output as numbered text ("optimized for LLMs"), style spans, JSON, HTML or SVG; query returns cursor, style, title and alt-screen state.
  • Agent integration: npx skills add mwunsch/termscope.

Core ideas:

  1. JSON-lines session protocol on stdio. A TUI driver that any harness can speak without an SDK or a daemon socket. mcp-tui-test: MCP over stdio plays the same role with a schema.
  2. Numbered-line text format for models. Row numbers in the text output so an agent can refer to a line without counting. mcp-tui-test: get_line(row) exists but capture_screen returns unnumbered text.
  3. Exit-code assertions for CI. exec --expect makes a one-liner a test. mcp-tui-test: assertion results are structured fields, not an exit code, because the caller is an MCP client.

docs.title: fcoury/termwright
docs.text:
github.com/fcoury/termwright · Rust · 23 stars · pushed 2026-02-10.

  • Approach: portable-pty and the vt100 crate, async (tokio). Library, CLI (run, screenshot, run-steps for YAML/JSON step files) and a daemon mode exposing a JSON-RPC Unix socket. Emulates replies to OSC 10/11/12 colour queries and CSI 6n cursor-position requests.
  • Assertions and snapshots: wait for text, regex, screen stability (wait_for_idle) or exit; screen as text or JSON with colours, cursor and cell attributes; PNG screenshots rendered with system fonts; box detection that finds UI boundaries from box-drawing characters.
  • Agent integration: JSON screen output described as "for AI agents"; no MCP server or skill.

Core ideas:

  1. Box detection. Deriving panel and dialog boundaries from box-drawing characters gives a semantic region without the app's cooperation. mcp-tui-test: regions are caller-specified coordinates.
  2. Declarative step files. A YAML or JSON scenario replaces a program for simple E2E flows. mcp-tui-test: no scenario format; the harness scripts calls.
  3. Shell-scriptable daemon. socat plus jq is enough to write tests. mcp-tui-test: needs an MCP client.

docs.title: charmbracelet/vhs
docs.text:
github.com/charmbracelet/vhs · Go · 21,201 stars · pushed 2026-10-01.

  • Approach: a .tape DSL (Type, Enter, Sleep, Wait /regex/, Set, Require, Hide/Show, Screenshot, Source, Env) executed against ttyd serving xterm.js in a headless Chromium driven by rod; frames are assembled by ffmpeg. vhs record writes a tape from a live session.
  • Assertions and snapshots: Output golden.ascii or .txt writes a text rendering for golden-file diffs in git; Wait[+Screen][+Line] /regex/ is the only synchronisation primitive. GIF, MP4, WebM and PNG frame outputs.
  • Agent integration: none built in. Agents use it to produce a GIF or .ascii they can read; testty compiles its scenarios to tapes for the same reason.

Core ideas:

  1. Tape DSL compiled to recordings. One short script yields a reproducible demo and a golden text file. mcp-tui-test: no DSL and no recording.
  2. Golden text outputs from the same run as the video. The .ascii render is the test; the GIF is the documentation. mcp-tui-test: no golden files.
  3. A real browser-hosted emulator. Rendering through xterm.js in Chromium makes the picture match what a web-embedded terminal shows, at the cost of heavy dependencies. mcp-tui-test: lightweight emulator, no pixels.

docs.title: charmbracelet x/exp/teatest
docs.text:
github.com/charmbracelet/x (package exp/teatest, with a v2 for Bubble Tea v2) · Go.

  • Approach: in-process. NewTestModel runs a tea.Model with a fake terminal size; Send(tea.Msg) injects messages; WaitFor(reader, cond) polls the output reader; FinalModel and FinalOutput wait for the program to quit.
  • Assertions and snapshots: RequireEqualOutput compares the final output bytes with a golden file in testdata/, updated with -update, diffed with the system diff.
  • Agent integration: none.

Core ideas:

  1. Golden output of the final frame. A single byte-exact file per test. mcp-tui-test: none.
  2. Inject messages, not keystrokes. Tests speak the framework's own event type, skipping the terminal. mcp-tui-test: always keystrokes through a PTY, which is what you want when the app is a black box.

docs.title: ratatui TestBackend with insta
docs.text:
ratatui.rs/recipes/testing/snapshots · Rust.

  • Approach: in-process. Terminal::new(TestBackend::new(80, 20)), draw the widget, assert_snapshot!(terminal.backend()). Snapshots are text, one row per line; colour is not included (ratatui issue #1402 is open for that). The recipe then points to termlens for the layers TestBackend cannot see: the event loop, raw mode, alternate screen, exit codes.
  • Agent integration: none.

Core ideas:

  1. In-process buffer snapshots with a review workflow. cargo insta review makes accepting intentional changes cheap. mcp-tui-test: none.
  2. Two layers, explicitly. Widget tests in-process, a few flows through a PTY. mcp-tui-test: is the second layer only.

docs.title: Textual Pilot and pytest-textual-snapshot
docs.text:
Textual testing guide and github.com/Textualize/pytest-textual-snapshot · Python · 52 stars · pushed 2025-04-26.

  • Approach: in-process. App.run_test() runs the app headless and yields a Pilot with press, click (by CSS selector or offset, with modifiers and click counts), hover and pause; size is set on run_test.
  • Assertions and snapshots: plain assert against widget state; snap_compare(app, press=[…], run_before=…, terminal_size=…) renders an SVG screenshot and compares it with the stored one; an HTML report shows the diff; --snapshot-update accepts changes.
  • Agent integration: none.

Core ideas:

  1. Selector-addressed interaction. pilot.click("#number-5") targets a widget, not a coordinate. Needs the framework's cooperation. mcp-tui-test: coordinates and text only.
  2. SVG screenshot as the snapshot artefact. Diffable in a browser, styles included. mcp-tui-test: none.

docs.title: pexpect / expect, pyte, libvterm
docs.text:
pexpect, expect, pyte, libvterm.

  • Approach: pexpect and expect spawn a PTY and match the byte stream against patterns; pyte (Python) and libvterm (C, used by Neovim) are VT emulators that turn that stream into a grid. mcp-tui-test's Python implementation is pexpect plus pyte.
  • Assertions: expect(pattern) with a timeout; pyte exposes screen.display, screen.buffer[row][col] with styles, and cursor; HistoryScreen adds scrollback.
  • Agent integration: none.

Core ideas:

  1. Stream matching for sequential programs. Cheap and exact when the program prints lines. mcp-tui-test: stream mode.
  2. Separate the PTY from the emulator. Any stream can be fed to any emulator. mcp-tui-test: same split (ScreenSession owns both).

docs.title: testty
docs.text:
docs.rs/testty, source in github.com/agentty-xyz/agentty (crates/testty) · Rust. The testty crate exists on crates.io (0.18.1 as of 2026-10-21); it is published from the agentty monorepo, and the latest crate-level description there is agentty's rather than testty's.

  • Approach: real PTY (portable-pty) with the vt100 crate. Scenario builder (wait_for_stable_frame, press_key, write_text, eventually, capture) run against a PtySessionBuilder; a testty run scenario.yaml CLI for non-Rust projects. Answers DA1 so capability probes return immediately.
  • Assertions and snapshots: match_text_in_region, recipes such as expect_selected_tab that read highlight styles; text or pixel baselines; "proof" reports as text, screenshot, GIF, HTML or JUnit XML. Feature GIFs are produced by compiling the same steps to a VHS .tape, hash-cached on the PTY frames and rendering settings so they re-record only when the UI changed.
  • Agent integration: none specific.

Core ideas:

  1. Semantic recipes over styles. "Selected tab" is defined by highlight attributes, not by text. mcp-tui-test: no style access.
  2. Compile scenarios to VHS tapes. The test and the demo recording are the same steps. mcp-tui-test: none.
  3. Hash-cached recordings. Re-render only when the frames changed. mcp-tui-test: none.

docs.title: hegner123/tui-test-ghost and mjpowersjr/vterm-mcp
docs.text:
github.com/hegner123/tui-test-ghost · Zig · 2 stars · pushed 2026-05-16. github.com/mjpowersjr/vterm-mcp · Rust · 3 stars · pushed 2026-04-15.

Both exist. Both are MCP servers over a real PTY and libghostty-vt, so they are the closest in shape to mcp-tui-test.

  • tui-test-ghost tools: tui_start, tui_send (key tokens such as down*3, with settle_ms), tui_screen, tui_cell (char, bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, dim, fg, bg), tui_wait (text, stable_ms, or cursor position), tui_resize, tui_snapshot (golden_path compares or creates a baseline), tui_stop, tui_record_start/stop to a JSONL file, and tui-test-ghost replay test.jsonl that re-executes action tools and compares assertion tools' recorded results. Every tool accepts a region.
  • vterm-mcp tools: start_session, stop_session, list_sessions, get_screen (text, cursor, optional per-cell styles), send_keys (named keys with C-, M-, S- prefixes), wait_for_text (substring or regex).

Core ideas:

  1. Record the MCP session, replay it as a test. The agent's exploratory calls become a JSONL file; replay re-runs the actions and checks the recorded assertion results, turning an interactive session into a regression test. mcp-tui-test: no recording.
  2. Region parameter on every read. Any tool can scope itself to a sub-rectangle, so screen text sent to the model stays small. mcp-tui-test: only get_screen_region.
  3. Golden snapshot as a tool. tui_snapshot with a path compares or creates the baseline from inside the agent loop. mcp-tui-test: none.
  4. Settle time on send. settle_ms and stable_ms wait for the screen to stop changing. mcp-tui-test: fixed delay.

docs.title: libghostty-vt and go-libghostty
docs.text:
mitchellh.com/writing/libghostty-is-coming (2025-09-22) and github.com/mitchellh/go-libghostty · Go bindings · 155 stars · pushed 2026-10-21 (a mirror; source of truth is on tangled.org).

libghostty-vt is "a zero-dependency library that provides an API for parsing terminal sequences and maintaining terminal state", extracted from Ghostty. It is the emulator under bombadil, ht, termscope, tui-test-ghost, vterm-mcp and one of the backends of microsoft/tui-test and termless. go-libghostty is a cgo binding that statically links it; its example feeds bytes to a Terminal and formats the grid as plain text with a Formatter.

Mitchell Hashimoto did not build a TUI test framework. On 2026-04-30 he wrote:

Libghostty can now be used to fuzz TUIs, thanks to @owickstrom + @AntithesisHQ. They already found bugs in multiple including btop. I always imagined libghostty would be useful for testing TUIs, super happy to see this is both practical and valuable.

This is another example of where speed matters! "Why does Ghostty need to be so fast?" Well, if you're running hundreds or thousands of unit tests that each use a clean in-memory terminal, you want that to be fast. If you're fuzz testing and trying to push an unlimited amount of data through a terminal, you want that terminal to be fast.

Core ideas:

  1. A production emulator as a library. The grid a test asserts on is the same code a real terminal renders, so emulator bugs are not the test's bugs. mcp-tui-test: pyte and vt10x are small independent emulators.
  2. Throughput as a testing feature. Fast parsing is what makes thousands of in-memory terminals per test run and fuzzing at hundreds of states per second practical. mcp-tui-test: one session per PTY, speed not a goal.

docs.title: Synthesis
docs.text:
Idea by tool. A filled cell means the tool has the idea as a documented feature. The last column is mcp-tui-test today.

Idea tui-test bombadil ht termless termlens termscope termwright vhs teatest ratatui Textual testty ghost / vterm-mcp mcp-tui-test Real PTY ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Production emulator (Ghostty, Alacritty, xterm.js, …) ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Multi-backend conformance ✓ ✓ Wait for idle / stable screen ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Wait on predicate over full screen state ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Frame-complete (DEC 2026) snapshots ✓ Locators returning match coordinates ✓ ✓ ✓ Cell styles and colours readable ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Region-scoped reads ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Semantic regions (box detection, tab recipes) ✓ ✓ ✓ Golden / snapshot comparison ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Grid masking of volatile cells ✓ SVG / PNG screenshots ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Recording (asciicast, GIF, tape) ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Replay a recording through the same assertions ✓ ✓ Tape / scenario DSL ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Answers terminal capability queries ✓ ✓ ✓ Mouse input ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Resize / SIGWINCH ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Scrollback ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Property-based exploration with shrinking ✓ Temporal properties over a trace ✓ Structured (JSON) results ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Failure artefacts beyond the message ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ partial MCP server ✓ ✓ ✓ Agent skill file ✓ ✓ ✓ Session daemon or server ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Live human view of the session ✓ ✓ In-process framework hooks ✓ ✓ ✓

"partial" for mcp-tui-test: failed assertions carry screen_excerpt; there are no traces, screenshots or recordings.

docs.title: Ideas mcp-tui-test could adopt next
docs.text:
Ordered by payoff for an agent-driven TUI test server, highest first. This is a list, not a plan; none of it is implemented.

  1. Wait for a stable screen. A wait_stable(quiet_ms) tool (termlens, ht --wait-idle, tui-test-ghost stable_ms) replaces the fixed delay on send_keys and the guesswork before capture_screen. It is the single most common cause of flaky agent runs and costs one loop over the buffer.
  2. Find text, return coordinates. A find_text(pattern) returning row and column spans (tui-test's locators, termlens's find_all) turns assert_at_position from "the caller guesses the position" into "the caller asserts what it found".
  3. Expose cell styles. pyte and vt10x both carry fg, bg, bold and reverse per cell; a get_cell(row, col) or a styled capture_screen lets an agent verify a selected item or an error colour (termless, tui-test-ghost tui_cell, testty's recipes).
  4. Record the tool calls, replay as a test. tui-test-ghost's JSONL recording and replay converts an agent's exploratory session into a deterministic pytest case with no extra authoring. The pytest plugin already has the engine for the replay side.
  5. Golden screen snapshots with grid masking. A snapshot(name) that compares the buffer text to a stored file, with termlens-style cell masks for clocks and PIDs, gives the pytest plugin a regression story and the MCP server a one-call assertion.
  6. Answer capability queries. Replying to CSI 6n, DA1 and DECRQM (termlens, termwright, testty) stops capability-probing apps from stalling on launch. Small code, removes a class of mysterious timeouts.
  7. Region on every read. A region parameter on capture_screen and the assertions (tui-test-ghost) keeps screen text sent to the model small without a second call.
  8. Resize. resize(cols, rows) with SIGWINCH (most tools) tests the layout path that in-process frameworks cannot reach.
  9. Default invariants. Bombadil's zero-config properties, "exited zero" and "never printed a replacement character", are cheap checks the registry could report on every close_session.
  10. An agent skill file. A SKILL.md describing when to use which mode and how to wait (the part ht says agents get wrong) complements the MCP schema for clients that load skills.
  11. Screenshots. SVG rendering of the buffer (termscope, termlens) gives a human a picture of what the agent saw. Useful, but the text grid already serves the model.
  12. Property-based exploration. Random action generation over the existing tools is possible from the harness side today; shrinking and temporal properties are Bombadil's whole product and out of scope for this server.
